title: Raft consensus
goal: By the end, you can implement Raft in Go from the paper and defend every rule in it: run elections, replicate and repair a log, explain the commit subtlety behind the paper's figure 8 and the single-server membership-change bug, take and restore snapshots, and serve linearizable and lease reads. You can also read production Raft code like etcd's raft package without drowning, know how practitioners test implementations with simulated partitions and fault injection, and reason about the performance and operations trade-offs real systems make on top of Raft.

lab.notes: Labs are small Go programs that simulate a Raft cluster inside one process: nodes as goroutines, a fake network that can delay, reorder and drop messages, and a disk as an in-memory or temp-dir file so fsync ordering can be exercised for real.

chapters.title: Why agreeing is hard
core_ideas: Replicated state machines: agree on one order of operations instead of every value
The crash-recovery fault model: lost and delayed messages, paused or rebooted servers, but no lying
Split brain in naive leader failover, and why fencing by wall clock fails
FLP in one paragraph: why Raft gives up guaranteed liveness and assumes partial synchrony
Majorities and quorum intersection as a counting trick
prereqs: Comfortable writing Go programs, and the idea of programs talking over a network. No distributed-systems background is assumed.

chapters.title: What survives a crash
core_ideas: Volatile versus durable state, and the three fields Raft must persist
The write-ahead log as a record you can replay after a reboot
fsync and the disk write cache: why write order, not write timing, decides correctness
Replaying a log on restart, and why replayed operations must be safe to repeat
prereqs: Chapter 1, and comfort with files and processes from building your container runtime. This chapter assumes no solid Linux-internals background and builds the durability ideas from scratch.

chapters.title: Terms, votes, and one leader at a time
core_ideas: Terms as a logical clock that makes stale leaders detectable
Randomized election timeouts and how they break split votes
Voting rules: one vote per term, majority to win, higher term always wins
The timing requirement broadcastTime << electionTimeout << MTBF
What a new leader must do before it knows the log: commit the no-op
prereqs: Chapters 1 and 2, including why persisted terms survive reboots.

chapters.title: One log, replicated
core_ideas: AppendEntries and the term and prevLogIndex/prevLogTerm consistency check
The log matching property and why induction makes it hold
commitIndex: a leader counts replicas, followers trust the leader's commitIndex
Applying entries to the state machine only after they are committed
Heartbeats as empty AppendEntries
prereqs: Chapter 3, including how a leader learns its term and log.

chapters.title: Repairing diverged logs
core_ideas: How follower logs diverge: gaps, uncommitted tails, and stale leaders
Walking nextIndex backward until the conflict is found
Forcing the follower to delete uncommitted suffixes
matchIndex and how the leader tracks each follower
The fast-backup optimization: sending enough terms to jump back in one round trip
prereqs: Chapter 4, including the AppendEntries check and the log matching property.

chapters.title: What committed really means
core_ideas: Two senses of committed, and why counting replicas is only safe for current-term entries
The paper's figure 8 scenario, traced step by step
Why a leader of term T may not decide commitment for term T' < T by counting replicas
The currentTerm check on AppendEntries, and leaders committing old entries indirectly
Where implementations got this wrong, from the Students' Guide and Raft Refloated
prereqs: Chapters 4 and 5, including how entries move and how followers check terms.

chapters.title: Why the safety argument holds
core_ideas: The election restriction: voting only for up-to-date logs
Leader completeness via the voting diagram argument: why a majority must hold any committed entry
State machine safety by induction over terms
The TLA+ spec as an executable version of the same argument
Where the informal proof is subtle: the ~90 invariants a machine-checked proof needed
prereqs: Chapters 3 and 6, including the figure 8 scenario and why only current-term entries count.

chapters.title: Changing the cluster while it runs
core_ideas: Why switching configuration one node at a time can split the cluster into two majorities
Joint consensus: two configuration entries, one leader for both
Single-server changes as the practical default and why they avoid the two-majority problem
The 2015 single-server-change bug and the fix: a leader appends config entries only after committing a current-term entry
Removed servers disrupting elections, and pre-vote as the mitigation
prereqs: Chapter 7, including why majorities intersect and what the election restriction guarantees.

chapters.title: Clients, sessions, and reads
core_ideas: Linearizability from the client's point of view, and why reads are not free
ReadIndex reads: going through the leader's committed position without the log
Lease reads and the clock assumptions they add
Client sessions and duplicate detection: exactly-once semantics on at-least-once retries
Stale follower reads and where they are acceptable
prereqs: Chapters 4 and 6, including commitIndex and what a committed entry guarantees.

chapters.title: Snapshots and forgetting the log
core_ideas: Why the log cannot grow forever, and what compaction throws away
What a snapshot contains: state machine state plus lastApplied and metadata
InstallSnapshot and the slow follower that has nothing left to catch up from
The paper's rule that a receiver discards its log on snapshot, and the bug real implementations made here
How snapshotting interacts with commit, replay, and restart
prereqs: Chapters 2, 4 and 5, including replay-on-restart and log repair.

chapters.title: Raft in the real world
core_ideas: How etcd's raft package is factored: the Ready loop, the Storage interface, transport and state machine left to the caller
Testing with simulated time: deterministic simulation and partition fault injection (Jepsen, Antithesis)
Performance levers: batching, pipelining, and inflight-message limits
Classic implementation bugs and what they teach about reading the rules precisely
How practitioners reason about Raft operations: quorum management, learners, and reconfiguration safety in etcd
prereqs: Chapters 4 through 10, since this chapter shows the whole machine as one library.
